0.title: 2 John: Truth and Love Are Not Opposites
0.overview:
Second John is one of the two shortest books in the New Testament — thirteen verses, about 245 words in the Greek, with only 3 John shorter — and one of the most compressed pastoral letters ever written. In the time it takes to read it aloud, the apostle John delivers a diagnosis, a doctrine, a commandment, and a warning that have shaped the church’s understanding of truth, love, and hospitality across twenty centuries. Do not let its brevity deceive you. Small letters can carry large weight.

The author identifies himself simply as “the elder” — not apostle, not prophet, not bishop, but presbyteros, the old man. By the time this letter was written (probably the 80s or 90s AD, during the same period as 1 John and Revelation), John was, by tradition, the last of the original apostles. He had outlived everyone. He carried a unique authority not just from his office but from his history: he had reclined next to Jesus at the Last Supper; he had stood at the foot of the cross; he had run to the empty tomb; he had seen the risen Lord. When this old man speaks, the church listens.

The letter is addressed to “the elect lady and her children.” Most scholars understand this as a metaphor for a local church and its members (a common early Christian way of speaking — the church as a woman, its members as her children; cf. 1 Peter 5:13 where “she who is at Babylon” is widely understood as the church at Rome). Some have understood it as an actual woman of prominence in the community. Either way, the letter was meant to circulate, to be read aloud, to reach the whole community.

The letter’s central concern is the same as 1 John’s: the threat of the deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. But 2 John adds a specific pastoral urgency: these deceivers are travelling teachers who expect to be received into the homes of the believers they visit. The letter’s famous prohibition — “Do not receive him into your house or give him any greeting” — has been misread as a licence for rudeness or suspicion of all strangers. It is not. It is the boundary-setting of a pastor who has watched false teachers exploit the church’s legendary hospitality to gain a platform for destroying what the gospel has built. Love, the elder insists, is not the opposite of truth. Love that abandons truth is not love; it is sentimentality in the service of deception.

1.title: Walk in Truth, Guard the Door
1.overview:
2 John moves in four steps: a greeting built on truth and love (vv. 1–3), joy at those walking in the truth and a renewed call to love (vv. 4–6), a warning against deceivers who deny that Christ came in the flesh (vv. 7–11), and a hope to meet face to face (vv. 12–13).

“Truth” appears five times in the first four verses. For John, truth is the reality of Jesus Christ, the Father’s Son, who truly became man. Love that is not shaped by that truth is not Christian love, and truth held without love is not Christian truth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greeting joins truth and love from its first line. The truth is not a theory we master and move beyond but a living reality in God’s people. Grace, mercy and peace come from the Father and the Son together.
verseByVerse.theology:
Truth and Love Together

Love that abandons truth is sentiment; truth without love is not the truth of the gospel. The Son is named in full, Jesus Christ, the Father’s Son, against those who divided him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church under pressure was told what bound it together.

Now: Christians of very different backgrounds belong to one another because they share the same truth about the same Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth, and not only I, but also all who know the truth, because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever: Grace, mercy, and peace will be with us, from God the Father and from Jesus Christ the Father's Son, in truth and love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 2 John is a short letter, about the length of a single sheet of papyrus, that applies the message of 1 John to one church. Its two great words are truth and love. The elder greets the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in the truth (vv. 1–3), rejoices that some are walking in the truth, and urges them to love one another, which means walking in God’s commands (vv. 4–6). But love must be guarded by truth: many deceivers deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, and the church must not welcome or support such teachers (vv. 7–11). The elder hopes to visit face to face (vv. 12–13). It is one of the smallest books in the Bible, and it guards the largest truth: that the eternal Son has come in our flesh.

The setting. “The elder” is traditionally the apostle John in old age. The style and themes are very close to 1 John, and early writers such as Irenaeus attributed it to the apostle. “Elder” suggests both his age and his standing; everyone knew who the elder was. Travelling preachers moved between house churches, and the churches depended on hospitality to support them. The false teachers of 1 John were using this hospitality to spread their errors.

The elder to the elect lady and her children. “Elect lady” (eklektē kyria) means chosen lady. It is most likely a figurative name for a local church, with her children being its members, and your elect sister (v. 13) being John’s own church. Churches were often pictured as women (Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 21:2), and the plural you in verses 6–12 supports this. Some think it was a Christian woman, perhaps named Kyria or Electa, and her family; either way, the counsel is for the whole household of God. And the first word about her is elect: before anything else is said about this church, it is said that God chose her.

Whom I love in truth. “In truth” (en alētheia) means truly, sincerely, and within the sphere of the truth of the gospel. Before love is commanded in this letter, it is grounded in truth. This is John’s answer to every sentimental Christianity that treats love as the dissolving of all distinctions. Love has a shape, and the shape is truth.

All who know the truth. A congregation is loved by Christians it has never met, because they share one truth and one Lord: a Christian abroad can walk into a strange church and find himself among family within minutes.

The truth that abides in us. Truth is said five times in verses 1–4, and here it is almost personified: the gospel, Christ himself (John 14:6), and the Spirit of truth (John 14:17), who abides in believers permanently. It is not a set of propositions we hold for a while; it holds us, and it will be with us when the world has gone.

Will be with us. Not a wish but a statement: will be. Paul’s greetings usually read as a prayer; John declares that they will have it. Grace deals with our guilt, mercy with our misery, peace with our estrangement, and all three are certain because their source is certain.

The Father’s Son. This is a unique phrase, found only here in the New Testament, emphasising Jesus’ relationship with the Father, against those who denied it (1 John 2:22–23). The blessings come equally from both, which no creature could share with God.

In truth and love. These are the two themes of the letter. Truth without love is a lamp held up to shame someone; love without truth is a warm room with the lights off. The Word became flesh, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). Jesus never traded one for the other: he told the Samaritan woman the truth about her five husbands in the same conversation in which he offered her living water (John 4:10–18), and he went to the cross both to honour God’s verdict on sin and to love sinners to the end. The church holds truth and love together because its Lord is both.

Does putting truth first not divide people? Would love not unite them better? Truth divides only what was never really united. A unity built on ignoring who Jesus is cannot last, because it has nothing at the centre; it is a crowd, not a family. The love John describes is stronger than mere agreement to get along, precisely because it rests on the truth that abides in us. That is why Christians of very different cultures, temperaments and politics can love one another deeply: they share the same Saviour. Real love tells the truth, and real truth is spoken in love (Ephesians 4:15). Each needs the other to be itself.
verseByVerse.note: “The elder” is traditionally the apostle John in old age. The “elect lady” is probably a local church and her “children” its members (see v. 13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Walk in Truth and Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The elder rejoices over those living out the truth day by day. Then he renews the old command to love one another, and defines love as walking in God’s commandments.
verseByVerse.theology:
Walk in Truth and Love

Love is walking according to God’s commandments, and the commandment is to walk in love. Each defines the other.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Some of the lady’s children were walking in the truth, and the elder rejoiced.

Now: Refuse the false choice between being loving and holding to the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: I rejoiced greatly to find some of your children walking in the truth, just as we were commanded by the Father. And now I ask you, dear lady—not as though I were writing you a new commandment, but the one we have had from the beginning—that we love one another. And this is love, that we walk according to his commandments; this is the commandment, just as you have heard from the beginning, so that you should walk in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of your children. “Some” (ek tōn teknōn sou) is literally some of your children: perhaps the ones John had met, or a quiet hint that not all were walking in truth. His joy and his concern live together. “Walking in the truth” is living consistently with the gospel, in belief and behaviour (3 John 3–4).

Walking in the one who is the truth. For John, truth is never only a set of correct statements; it is a person. Jesus said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). To walk in the truth is therefore to walk in him, as Paul puts it: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him (Colossians 2:6). The children who made the old apostle glad were not simply orthodox; they were walking along the road that Christ himself is.

Just as we were commanded by the Father. Walking in truth is God’s command, not an option. Yet the Father who requires it first gave the truth, and the Spirit of truth who abides in us (v. 2) keeps us walking in it.

And now I ask you, dear lady. The last apostle, with all the authority of one who saw the Lord, chooses the language of a request.

Not a new commandment. As in 1 John 2:7, the command to love is not a novelty, unlike the false teachers’ new ideas. It is Jesus’ own command (John 13:34), and John’s we puts himself under it with them.

This is love. Love is defined by obedience (1 John 5:3; John 14:15). Love is not a vague feeling that does as it pleases; it walks in God’s ways.

A circle. Love means obeying God’s commands, and God’s command is to love. It is an illuminating circle, not a vicious one, and we live neither perfectly. Only the Son loved the Father and his own without a single failure, and because his obedience is counted as ours, our uneven love is received in him.

Some of my children are not walking in the truth. What do I do with that grief? You are in good company: the elder knew it, and so did the Father of the prodigal son. Keep praying for them, and never stop; Monica prayed for Augustine for many years before he came to Christ. Keep loving them visibly, and keep the door open, while not pretending that their path is right. Do not carry a guilt that is not yours: you are responsible for your faithfulness, not for their hearts, which only God can change. Rejoice over the children who do walk in the truth, as John did. And leave the others in the hands of the Father, who is a better parent than you and goes out looking for the lost.

In everyday life. Tell someone younger in the faith that you have noticed him walking in the truth. Few things encourage a believer more than hearing that an older Christian has seen and rejoiced.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love has boundaries. Many deceivers have gone out who deny “the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh”, that the eternal Son truly became man. If he was not truly human, his death cannot atone for human sin. John warns the church not to lose what the apostles built in them, and forbids giving these teachers a platform.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guarding the Door

Deceivers deny the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. To host and bless such a teacher is to take part in his work.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: House churches hosted and supported travelling teachers.

Now: The church must not give a platform to anyone who denies who Christ is, and every member shares the duty to watch.

verseByVerse.quote: For many deceivers have gone out into the world, those who do not confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Such a one is the deceiver and the antichrist. Watch yourselves, so that you may not lose what we have worked for, but may win a full reward. Everyone who goes on ahead and does not abide in the teaching of Christ, does not have God. Whoever abides in the teaching has both the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many deceivers. “Deceivers” (planoi) are those who lead astray. “Gone out” is perhaps from the church (1 John 2:19; 4:1): the deceivers are not strangers; they once belonged.

The coming in the flesh. The phrase (erchomenon en sarki) is a present participle: coming in the flesh. They denied that the eternal Christ truly became human (1 John 4:2).

The deceiver and the antichrist. As in 1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3. The spirit of antichrist is already at work in every denial of who Jesus is, and Scripture also speaks of a final figure (2 Thessalonians 2:3–8).

Watch yourselves. “What we have worked for” is the fruit of the apostles’ labour among them (some manuscripts read what you have worked for). A farmer who has laboured a whole season does not leave the gate open the week before harvest.

A full reward. “Full reward” (misthon plērē) means full wages. Faithfulness will be rewarded in full (1 Corinthians 3:8, 14). God is no man’s debtor, and he does not underpay.

Goes on ahead. The false teachers thought themselves advanced thinkers who had moved beyond the crude literalism of the incarnation. John names their progress for what it is: leaving the teaching of Christ. “Teaching of Christ” is both the teaching about Christ and the teaching Christ gave. It is the boundary within which the Christian church lives.

Both the Father and the Son. To abandon the truth about Christ is to lose God himself (1 John 2:23). To abide in the apostolic teaching is to have both the Father and the Son; to go beyond it is to have neither.

The road and the cliff. Picture a mountain road with a sheer drop on one side. A driver who goes beyond the edge of the road is not making progress; he is falling. Progress in the Christian life is real, but it always happens on the road: deeper into Christ, not past him. Every generation produces teachers who offer to take believers further than the apostles went. John’s answer is that past the apostles there is only air.

Can a believer, then, lose his salvation? What John warns of losing is what we have worked for, the fruit of the apostles’ labour in them, and the fullness of reward. Arminian Christians, who believe that a true believer can finally fall away, read the warning as a threat to salvation itself. The more likely reading is that true believers are kept by God, but may lose much by being led astray, and the warning is one of the means by which he keeps them watchful. John has already said that those who left the church showed that they had never truly belonged (1 John 2:19), and Jesus says that no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28). Faithful Christians differ on this, and both sides take the warning seriously.

What does going on ahead look like today? It usually presents itself as maturity. It says the church has outgrown old ideas: that Jesus need not be God, that his resurrection need not be bodily, that sin and judgment are primitive notions, that the apostles were men of their time whose views we have moved past. It may keep the vocabulary of faith while emptying it. The test is simple: does this teaching stay within what Christ and his apostles taught, or does it claim to improve on them? Any message that leaves you with a smaller Christ than the New Testament gives you has gone on ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house or give him any greeting, for whoever greets him takes part in his wicked works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone comes. The setting is essential: the church met in homes, and the host of the house church was also the host of any travelling teacher. To receive a teacher into your home was to endorse his ministry: to give him bed, board and a pulpit (3 John 5–8).

Into your house. Probably the house church, though the home itself is included. Do not be the platform, the endorsement or the sponsor for the denial of the incarnation.

Any greeting. “Greeting” (chairein) is not ordinary politeness but the formal welcome that signalled acceptance as a Christian teacher, a blessing on his work; the King James Version renders it God speed. To give that blessing to someone actively spreading a false gospel is to take part in the spreading.

Takes part. “Takes part” (koinōnei) means shares in, partners with. It is the verb of fellowship, the same family as koinōnia in 1 John 1:3. Fellowship is precious, and it can be given to the wrong thing.

What the closed door protects. John is not guarding a private club; he is guarding a person. The teaching these travellers carried denied that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (v. 7), and with it the cross, for a Christ without a body has no blood to shed. To house and bless such a teacher would be to sponsor an attack on the Saviour himself, and on the very thing that saves the sheep. Paul told the Ephesian elders that fierce wolves would come in among them, not sparing the flock (Acts 20:29), and he wept as he warned them. The closed door is love for Christ and for the people he bought with his blood (Acts 20:28).

Where Christians differ: does this forbid all kindness to those who hold false beliefs? Some have used this verse to justify refusing even basic courtesy or hospitality to anyone outside their group. This commentary’s view: John is forbidding the church to welcome, platform and support teachers who deny the incarnation, giving them the endorsement of Christian fellowship. He is not forbidding kindness, courtesy or evangelism toward unbelievers, or even toward those in error. Jesus ate with sinners (Luke 15:2), and believers must love their neighbours and enemies (Luke 6:27). The line is between loving people and endorsing their false teaching.

Does this mean I should refuse to speak with Jehovah’s Witnesses or Mormons at the door? John forbids welcoming false teachers into the church’s homes and supporting their work, which is what a greeting and hospitality meant for travelling teachers then. It does not forbid speaking to them, explaining the gospel or treating them with courtesy. What a Christian should not do is give them a platform or help them spread a message that denies Christ’s deity.

And what of a family member who has joined a cult? This verse concerns travelling teachers, not family. Keep loving contact, pray, and bear witness, while refusing to endorse or support their teaching. This also fits Paul’s call to correct opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:24–25): gentleness toward the person, firmness about the teaching.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes and depended on travelling teachers; to host a teacher was to give him a platform.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The elder has more to say, but would rather say it face to face, “so that our joy may be complete.” The greeting from “the children of your elect sister” shows one church greeting another: the church is a family of families.
verseByVerse.theology:
Face to Face

Letters carry the truth; presence completes the joy of fellowship.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The children of a sister church sent their greetings.

Now: No congregation stands alone, and no screen replaces being together.

verseByVerse.quote: Though I have much to write to you, I would rather not use paper and ink. Instead I hope to come to you and talk face to face, so that our joy may be complete. The children of your elect sister greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paper and ink. A sheet of papyrus and ink of soot and gum. The elder’s reluctance to say everything in writing is not evasiveness but pastoral wisdom. The letter has said what could not wait: the warning, the boundary, the call to abide. The rest requires presence.

Face to face. “Face to face” (stoma pros stoma) is literally mouth to mouth. Letters are good, but fellowship in person is better.

Our joy complete. As in 1 John 1:4, the phrase borrows from Jesus’ prayer, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves (John 17:13). It is a foretaste of the final gathering, when we shall see him face to face and know as we are known (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Your elect sister. The church is a family of churches: two congregations, miles apart, are sisters, both chosen, both loved, both belonging to the same Father.

Is online fellowship enough? It is a gift, especially for the housebound, the persecuted and those far away, and God uses it. John himself used a letter. But he did not want the letter to replace the visit. There are things that happen only when believers are in the same room: shared bread and wine, a hand on a shoulder, a face that tells you more than words, singing together, being noticed when you are absent. If you are able to gather with God’s people in person, do not settle for a screen. If you are not able, ask the church to come to you.

For worship. God himself did not send only a letter. He spoke through prophets for centuries, and then the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. One day the Lamb will come for his bride, and we shall see his face, and our joy will be complete, because the one we have known by letter will be with us in person for ever.
